newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom buyers maybe disappointed.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom buyers maybe disappointed.

text.p: Managers of Europe's largest-ever share offering, next week's sale of Deutsche Telekom stock, are bracing themselves for a wave of investor discontent.
Because of enormous demand, the $12 billion issue is expected to be oversubscribed several times and as a result only a fraction of total orders can be filled.
This could leave many private investors disappointed as they get far fewer Telekom shares than ordered.
Anticipating complaints from angry investors, lead underwriter, Deutsche Bank AG, has set up a hot-line to try to ensure that first-time investors do not go away mad.
"We presume that not every investor will be able to receive the full allotment," Deutsche Bank spokesman Roland Weichert told Reuters.

"We will offer specific consulting afterwards with investors who did not receive their full allocation to point out alternatives, such as buying Telekom shares on the market or making other investments."

The subscription period for Telekom's share offering ends on Thursday. The company will float up to 690 million shares, with trade beginning in Germany and New York on November 18 and a day later in Tokyo.

Telekom's 100-million-mark ($67 million) advertising campaign has whipped up such interest in the issue that more than three million Germans signed up with the company to buy shares, over half of these have never owned stocks before.
Investors have been required to buy a minimum of 100 Telekom shares. But now there is speculation that will also be a maximum number because of high demand.

The banks are concerned that the masses of first-time shareholders that have gathered for Telekom's listing will become frustrated and dash hopes that the issue could become a watershed event creating broad public equity holdings.
The first rumblings of investor discontent began after Telekom unexpectedly topped up the issue on Monday with the placement of up to 115 million additional shares.

The Association for the Protection of Shareholders (DSW), Germany's largest shareholder's rights lobby, slammed Telekom for fattening the issue, saying it would weaken investor earnings potential and alienate first-time shareholders.
"The huge advertising success has led Telekom to seize the opportunity and ruthlessly exploit it," DSW said in a statement.

The shareholders' lobby group said private investors who signed on early would see their dividends watered down and that the potential for a rise in Telekom's share price was reduced because institutional investors would receive extra shares.
Tight supply for institutional investors was expected to be the main factor that would drive Telekom's share price up soon after the offering.
DSW said Telekom's moves to take some of the wind out of the sails of its new shares "do not serve to build trust for new shareholders and damage Germany as a financial centre".
Deutsche Telekom, however, rejected the criticism. It said the additional shares would have little impact on share price developments and that it would not change dividend policy.
It is also not unusual for companies to add shares to an initial public offering shortly before the placement if demand exceeds expectations.
Sporting goods maker Adidas AG last year topped up its IPO with 4.6 million additional shares to 27.3 million just four days ahead of the issue.
"This kind of thing happens all the time with stock offerings," said Deutsche Bank's Weichert.
